proposed_title: Trump Removes State Department Inspector General Steve Linick
proposed_description_short: Trump removed State Department IG Steve Linick in May 2020 amid inquiries involving Mike Pompeo; motive remains disputed.
proposed_description_medium: Congressional statements and a subsequent inquiry confirm Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick in May 2020. Linick’s office had inquiries involving Secretary Mike Pompeo. Lawmakers alleged retaliation; Pompeo denied knowing about one inquiry, and the administration cited lack of confidence. The supplied USA Today link is an unrelated wildfire story and cannot support this entry.
proposed_description_long: President Donald Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick in May 2020. The congressional record and the congressional inquiry into the removal document that Linick’s office had several open matters involving Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, including review of the emergency arms-sale process and a separate inquiry concerning use of department staff for personal tasks. Lawmakers said they were investigating whether the dismissal was retaliatory. That allegation must remain attributed: the existence of pending inquiries and the timing of the removal do not by themselves prove motive. Pompeo said he recommended Linick’s removal and denied knowing about one investigation; the White House’s notification cited the president’s lack of confidence. The source URL attached to this row is an unrelated 2026 Oklahoma wildfire forecast and supplies no evidence for the personnel action. Replace it with the congressional records or contemporaneous reporting before publication. A defensible description can state the removal and the documented oversight context while distinguishing the competing accounts of the reason.

proposed_title: Trump Pardons Steven Benjamin Floyd on January 19, 2021
proposed_description_short: Trump Pardons Steven Benjamin Floyd on January 19, 2021
proposed_description_medium: The Justice Department’s clemency list records that Donald Trump pardoned Steven Benjamin Floyd on January 19, 2021. It identifies Floyd’s 2008 Southern District of Mississippi conviction for bank robbery by extortion and lists a sentence of 30 months, with the final six months in a halfway house, three years of supervised release and a $2,500 fine. The index establishes the conviction label, sentence and pardon date, but gives no account of the underlying offense or the reason for clemency. No motive should be inferred from the grant alone.
proposed_description_long: The Department of Justice’s Office of the Pardon Attorney lists Steven Benjamin Floyd among the pardons President Donald Trump granted on January 19, 2021. The official record identifies the federal offense, sentencing court and date, and sentence imposed. This supports the clemency action and the case details as DOJ records them. The list does not describe the underlying robbery, identify a victim, or explain Trump’s rationale for granting the pardon. A grounded account should state the pardon date and listed conviction information without adding an unsupported account of the conduct or a claim of favoritism. The cited records supply enough detail to report the public clemency action, but no more. The records do not support an explanation of why the president selected Floyd for clemency or establish that the pardon was improper. The DOJ list is limited to clemency data and should not be read as a narrative of the offense or a reasoned account of the decision.

proposed_title: New York Times Raises Questions About Trump’s Role in Texas Runoffs
proposed_description_short: A March 4, 2026, New York Times analysis asks how Trump may affect Texas runoffs; the accessible excerpt identifies only part of its four-question framing.
proposed_description_medium: The linked New York Times article is a March 4, 2026, analysis of Texas politics after the primaries, not a report of a Trump action. A syndicated excerpt identifies questions about whether Trump would join an effort against Ken Paxton and how a Texas House runoff could affect Republicans. The Texas Tribune reported that John Cornyn and Paxton advanced to a Republican Senate runoff and James Talarico won the Democratic nomination. The NYT article body was inaccessible, so the remaining questions cannot be summarized reliably.
proposed_description_long: The linked New York Times page is titled “What’s Next for Texas Under Trump? 4 Big Questions.” The accessible syndicated excerpt identifies two parts of that analysis: whether Trump would join a “Stop-Paxton” effort in the Republican Senate runoff, and whether a Texas House runoff would become a problem for Republicans. Separately, the Texas Tribune’s March 4, 2026, primary-results account reported that Republican Sen. John Cornyn and Attorney General Ken Paxton were headed to a runoff, while state Rep. James Talarico won the Democratic Senate nomination. These are election results and questions about possible political strategy; they do not establish that Trump endorsed a candidate, intervened in the runoff, or caused a policy outcome. The NYT article itself returned HTTP 403 in this review, and the syndicated excerpt does not expose all four questions. A full article text or a complete reliable synopsis is still needed before this record can be presented as a comprehensive summary. It should be treated as political analysis, not a standalone Trump action.

proposed_title: Village Voice reported on a 1988 inquiry into Trump Tower apartment financing
proposed_description_short: Wayne Barrett’s Village Voice investigation recounted an inquiry into two Trump Tower apartment purchases and Giuliani fundraising.
proposed_description_medium: The Village Voice’s 2019 archive republishes Wayne Barrett’s 1993 reporting on a federal inquiry into Trump Tower purchases by Robert Hopkins. Barrett wrote that agent Tony Lombardi interviewed Trump twice about the financing; weeks later, Trump publicly offered to raise $2 million for Rudy Giuliani if Giuliani ran for mayor. The article says Lombardi closed the inquiry, but the available record does not establish that the pledge caused the decision or prove money laundering.
proposed_description_long: Wayne Barrett’s Village Voice investigation, originally published in 1993 and republished in 2019, examined a 1988 federal inquiry into the financing of two Trump Tower apartments purchased by Robert Hopkins. Barrett reported that Hopkins struggled to document income, that Trump signed a bond connected to Hopkins’s deposit, and that agent Tony Lombardi conducted two hour-long interviews with Trump about the sale. Within weeks, the story says, Trump announced he could raise $2 million if then-U.S. Attorney Rudy Giuliani ran for mayor; Trump later co-chaired a Giuliani fundraiser. Barrett reported that Lombardi closed the inquiry without assigning it a case number, and the Village Voice editor frames that closure as a favor to Trump. This is an attributed investigative account, not a reproduced federal case file or court finding. It supports an entry about what the Village Voice reported and the sequence it described, not a conclusion that Trump committed money laundering or that fundraising caused Giuliani or Lombardi to end an investigation. Later articles cite Barrett’s original reporting; they do not independently corroborate every allegation.

proposed_title: Brian Murphy’s Complaint Alleges DHS Officials Sought Changes to Threat Assessments
proposed_description_short: Brian Murphy’s 2020 whistleblower complaint alleged DHS leaders pressed for changes to threat assessments involving white supremacists and Antifa; the claims are allegations.
proposed_description_medium: Brian Murphy filed a whistleblower reprisal complaint with DHS’s inspector general on September 8, 2020. The House Intelligence Committee’s release says he alleged that Ken Cuccinelli sought to soften the white-supremacist section of a Homeland Threat Assessment and add discussion of violent left-wing groups; Murphy also alleged requests to align Antifa assessments with President Trump’s public remarks. These are complaint allegations, not findings.
proposed_description_long: On September 8, 2020, Brian Murphy, then a senior official in the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Intelligence and Analysis, filed a whistleblower reprisal complaint with the DHS inspector general. The House Intelligence Committee released the complaint the next day. In it, Murphy alleged that in May and June 2020, acting deputy secretary Ken Cuccinelli asked him to change the Homeland Threat Assessment so that the white-supremacist threat appeared less severe and information about violent left-wing groups was included. Murphy also alleged that, during meetings from late May through July, Cuccinelli and acting secretary Chad Wolf directed him to modify intelligence assessments concerning Antifa and “anarchist” groups to align with President Trump’s public comments. The complaint records Murphy’s allegations and his account that he declined to make changes based on political rhetoric. It does not itself establish an inspector-general or congressional finding that the officials issued the instructions or that the assessments were changed. The original TrumpFile summary did not provide this primary document; the committee release and complaint support an attributed allegation rather than a proven cover-up.
